strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: measuring graded human contribution in AI-assisted writing. Its explicit focus on informational contribution, with limitations separating this from creativity and legal authorship, provides a useful research scope.

The proposed score is simple to compute from conditional and unconditional token probabilities. The manuscript explains the approach clearly and supplies dataset sources, generation prompts, model identifiers, and threshold-selection details.

The experiments have substantial breadth: 2,000 source entries per domain across four domains, multiple generation and surrogate models, repeated generations, and analyses of length, style, and temperature. Consistent ordering across broad prompting categories supports the score as a useful coarse signal.

The human study provides encouraging evidence within its selected sample: 1,500 pairs receive three independent judgments, with 91.47% unanimous agreement and 95.93% agreement between majority judgments and the input-aware score. The WildChat evaluation also extends coverage to actual user interactions.
weaknesses: The central information-theoretic interpretation needs stronger justification. Equation (5) computes a pointwise log-likelihood ratio; mutual information requires an expectation under a joint distribution. Moreover, the unconditional language-model distribution is not shown to equal the output marginal induced by human prompts. The pointwise score can be negative even when the generating model is known. Consequently, normalization by output surprisal does not itself establish a percentage of information attributable to humans. This affects the interpretation of the measure, beyond terminology.

The text-only extension does not establish the claimed minimum. Appendix B derives a lower bound conditional on a chosen plausibility threshold, but Equation (10) does not demonstrate that any prompt attains that bound. Setting the threshold using mean conditional surprisal plus one standard deviation provides no reported coverage or tightness guarantee on target data. Furthermore, writing h = I(y)/N and c = -log(tau), the estimator is exactly 1 - c/h. For a fixed model and threshold, it ranks texts identically to ordinary mean unconditional negative log-likelihood. Table 2's detection AUCs therefore do not independently validate the minimum-contribution interpretation. This equivalence, bound tightness, and calibration sensitivity require explicit treatment.

The main validation cannot establish general ranking accuracy or calibrated percentages. Section 5.1 selects only pairs separated by more than 0.1 under the proposed metric, excluding comparisons where it predicts small differences. Both reported human-agreement results inherit this selection. The synthetic hierarchy also systematically varies prompt length and input-output overlap, yet there are no simple length, lexical-overlap, or semantic-similarity baselines. Score-independent sampling, comparisons within generation categories, matched controls, and uncertainty estimates are needed to establish what the metric contributes beyond these correlates.

Several practical claims exceed the supporting tests. The two fixed instructions in Appendix C.3 provide limited evidence about adaptive attacks because they are not optimized against the score. WildChat category differences provide indirect validation without instance-level contribution judgments. In the multi-round study, asking the model to correct hallucinations supplies no verified factual corrections from a human; an increased score after model self-correction therefore does not establish increased human informational contribution.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendix. The submission does not link scoring code or the constructed and annotated datasets, and it leaves consequential probability-computation details unspecified, including the unconditional context, chat formatting, special-token treatment, and whether scoring probabilities incorporate generation temperature. The promising category-level findings merit further development, but the measurement interpretation, independent validation, and reproducibility gaps warrant revision before a Findings recommendation.
